passages.title: The Bell on the Door
passages.content:
When the repair shop opened on Saturday, Eva noticed that its doorbell no longer rang. Her grandfather had used the little bell for years to hear customers arriving while he worked in the back room. Without it, he kept leaving his bench to check the empty doorway. Eva offered to help, but he handed her a box of receipts to sort instead. She stacked the papers quickly, hoping he would see that she could manage a more interesting job.

After lunch, a customer stood quietly by the counter until Eva greeted him. Her grandfather came forward carrying a half-finished clock. He apologized and looked up at the silent bell. Eva asked whether she could examine it while he spoke with the customer. This time he nodded. The cord was not broken; it had slipped from a small metal hook. Eva climbed onto a steady stool, put the cord back, and pulled the door open. The bell gave one bright ring.

Her grandfather returned to his bench, then paused. He placed a screwdriver beside the receipt box and showed Eva how to choose the right tip. She moved the tool away from the edge of the counter so it would not fall. Later, when the next customer arrived, her grandfather stayed at his bench long enough to finish a delicate adjustment. Eva answered the bell herself. She did not announce that she had proved anything. She simply asked the customer what needed repairing.

plans.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Eva earns greater responsibility by solving a practical problem.
Eva teaches her grandfather to repair clocks.
The shop stops serving customers because its bell breaks.
Eva decides that sorting receipts is the shop’s most important job.
reasons: Her repair leads her grandfather to give her a tool and let her greet a customer.
The grandfather is already repairing a clock; Eva repairs the bell’s cord.
Customers continue to arrive and receive help.
Eva initially wants a task beyond sorting receipts.
plans.evidence: He placed a screwdriver beside the receipt box and showed Eva how to choose the right tip.
plans.why: The new tool and instruction show the increased trust Eva earns after repairing the bell.
plans.method: Connect the initial problem, Eva’s action, and the responsibility she receives afterward.
plans.trap: A detail about clocks is not the central event.

plans.prompt: Why had the doorbell stopped ringing?
choices: Its cord had slipped from a metal hook.
A customer had removed its cord.
Its cord had broken in two.
Eva’s grandfather had taken the bell down.
reasons: The passage directly identifies the slipped cord as the problem.
No customer removes the cord.
The passage explicitly says the cord was not broken.
The bell remains on the door.
plans.evidence: The cord was not broken; it had slipped from a small metal hook.
plans.why: This sentence gives the physical cause of the silent bell.
plans.method: Locate the sentence explaining the bell’s condition rather than guessing from its silence.
plans.trap: A silent object is not necessarily broken.

plans.prompt: Why does Eva initially sort the receipts quickly?
choices: She hopes to show that she is ready for a more interesting task.
She wants to leave the shop before customers arrive.
She believes the receipts will repair the bell.
She has promised a customer that she will finish a clock.
reasons: The narrator states that she hopes her grandfather will recognize her ability.
Eva stays and asks to help with the bell.
She does not treat the receipts as a repair.
No such promise is described.
plans.evidence: She stacked the papers quickly, hoping he would see that she could manage a more interesting job.
plans.why: Her speed is meant to demonstrate readiness, not to end her workday.
plans.method: Look for what the character hopes to accomplish by performing the action.
plans.trap: Finishing a task quickly can serve a goal other than leaving.

plans.prompt: What happens immediately after Eva puts the cord back on its hook?
choices: She opens the door and hears the bell ring.
Her grandfather gives her the receipt box.
The customer enters carrying a clock.
Her grandfather shows her how to select a screwdriver tip.
reasons: Opening the door tests the repair directly after she replaces the cord.
The receipt task occurs before lunch.
No clock carried in by that customer is described.
The screwdriver instruction occurs later.
plans.evidence: Eva climbed onto a steady stool, put the cord back, and pulled the door open.
plans.why: The actions are narrated in order; opening the door is the next action after replacing the cord.
plans.method: Trace the action verbs around the event named in the question.
plans.trap: A later consequence is not the immediately following event.

plans.prompt: How does the shop’s layout contribute to the problem in the passage?
choices: The back workroom makes it difficult for the grandfather to notice customers without the bell.
The counter is too high for any customer to speak to Eva.
The stool prevents the door from opening.
The grandfather’s bench is outside the shop.
reasons: He relies on the bell to hear arrivals while working in the back.
The counter does not stop Eva from greeting the customer.
The stool is used safely during the repair.
The bench is in the back workroom.
plans.evidence: Her grandfather had used the little bell for years to hear customers arriving while he worked in the back room.
plans.why: The separated work area explains why a silent doorbell interrupts his work.
plans.method: Connect a physical feature of the setting to the difficulty it creates for a character.
plans.trap: Do not invent a physical obstacle merely because an object is mentioned.

plans.prompt: What does the grandfather’s later decision to give Eva a screwdriver most strongly suggest?
choices: He is becoming more willing to trust her with practical work.
He no longer intends to repair any clocks.
He believes she caused the cord to slip off its hook.
He wants her to stop greeting customers.
reasons: The tool and instruction follow her successful repair and contrast with the earlier receipt-sorting assignment.
He returns to his bench and later finishes a delicate adjustment, so he continues repairing clocks.
No evidence suggests Eva caused the original problem.
Eva later answers the bell and greets the next customer herself.
plans.evidence: He placed a screwdriver beside the receipt box and showed Eva how to choose the right tip.
plans.why: Giving a practical tool and guidance after her repair supports increased trust; the passage does not directly state his private thoughts.
plans.method: Connect the exact clue to its surrounding actions or argument; distinguish what is stated from the conclusion it supports.
plans.trap: A defensible inference follows from the text without adding an unsupported motive, guarantee, or universal claim.

passages.title: Water in the Bag
passages.content:
A dry, clear bag tied loosely around a leafy branch can reveal a process that is usually invisible. After the bag has been left in place for a time, tiny drops may appear on its inner surface. The branch has not become a raincloud. The drops are evidence that water moved from the plant into the air inside the bag and then returned to liquid form on the bag’s surface.

A plant takes in water through its roots. Water moves through its tissues, and some of it leaves through tiny openings in the leaves as water vapor. That release is called transpiration. Water vapor is a gas and cannot be seen as separate drops. When it changes back into liquid water, the change is called condensation. The drops in the bag make the result of that change visible.

The demonstration is more useful when the observer asks where else the water might have come from. Rain already on a leaf could supply drops without showing water released by the plant. A bag placed around wet leaves would therefore be harder to interpret. Starting with dry leaves helps reduce that confusion. Comparing the leafy branch with an empty, equally dry bag also helps the observer decide whether the leaves made a difference.

The bag does not measure every part of the water cycle, and one observation cannot tell us how much water every plant releases. It offers a small window on one process. Its value lies in linking an unfamiliar explanation to an observation that a person can examine carefully.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea?
choices: A simple bag demonstration can make a plant’s release of water observable, but the result must be interpreted carefully.
Plants create rainclouds inside clear bags.
Every plant releases the same amount of water.
A bag measures every part of the water cycle.
reasons: The passage explains both the observable process and the need to check alternative sources of water.
The first paragraph explicitly rejects this explanation.
The final paragraph limits what one observation can show.
The passage explicitly says the bag does not measure every part.
plans.evidence: Its value lies in linking an unfamiliar explanation to an observation that a person can examine carefully.
plans.why: The demonstration matters because it connects a process to inspectable evidence, with limits described in the preceding paragraphs.
plans.method: Include both the explained process and the cautions developed later in the passage.
plans.trap: A central idea should include the passage’s qualifications.

plans.prompt: What causes water vapor to become visible as drops on the bag?
choices: The vapor changes back into liquid water.
The roots turn into small clouds.
The leaves create a hole in the bag.
The bag measures the weight of the branch.
reasons: The change from vapor to liquid is condensation, producing visible drops.
No roots or clouds form in the bag.
A hole does not explain the liquid drops.
No weighing is performed.
plans.evidence: When it changes back into liquid water, the change is called condensation.
plans.why: Condensation produces the visible liquid described in the demonstration.
plans.method: Distinguish the plant’s release of vapor from the later change that produces liquid drops.
plans.trap: Transpiration and condensation are different steps.

plans.prompt: In the last paragraph, what does “a small window on one process” mean?
choices: A limited way to observe and understand one process.
A hole cut into the bag to let air escape.
A glass frame attached to the branch.
A complete explanation of every kind of weather.
reasons: The paragraph contrasts a useful observation with the limits of what it can reveal.
The phrase describes understanding rather than a literal hole.
No frame is attached to the plant.
The paragraph expressly limits the demonstration to one process.
plans.evidence: The bag does not measure every part of the water cycle, and one observation cannot tell us how much water every plant releases.
plans.why: The stated limits make “window” a figurative opportunity to observe, rather than a complete view of the water cycle.
plans.method: Use the limiting sentences around the phrase to determine its figurative meaning.
plans.trap: A familiar word can be used figuratively rather than literally.

plans.prompt: Which detail most directly supports the need to start with dry leaves?
choices: Water already on a leaf could produce drops without showing water released by the plant.
The bag is clear.
A branch contains leaves.
Water vapor is a gas.
reasons: This explains the competing source of drops that dry leaves help rule out.
Clarity helps observation but does not explain why the leaves must start dry.
The presence of leaves does not distinguish the two water sources.
The state of vapor does not by itself explain the dry-leaf control.
plans.evidence: Rain already on a leaf could supply drops without showing water released by the plant.
plans.why: Starting dry reduces the chance of mistaking existing surface water for water released by the plant.
plans.method: Identify which detail explains the specific control named in the question.
plans.trap: A relevant science fact is not always evidence for the specific claim.

plans.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: An observable demonstration can help explain a plant process when competing explanations and limits are considered.
The bag proves that every plant releases water at the same rate.
The best observation is one made with wet leaves and no comparison.
A plant’s roots form the visible drops without releasing vapor.
reasons: The passage develops the mechanism, the dry-leaf comparison, and the limits of one observation.
The ending explicitly rejects that conclusion from one observation.
Existing water makes the source of drops harder to interpret.
Water first moves into the air as vapor and later condenses.
plans.evidence: It offers a small window on one process.
plans.why: The useful observation is limited; understanding it requires the preceding mechanism and control explanations.
plans.method: Combine the process explanation with the caution developed in the later paragraphs.
plans.trap: A main idea should preserve an informational passage’s limits.

plans.prompt: Why would drops in an empty comparison bag make the leafy-bag result harder to interpret?
choices: They would show that drops can appear in this setup without a leafy branch.
They would prove that the plant has no roots.
They would establish the exact rate of transpiration for every plant.
They would make liquid water impossible inside the leafy bag.
reasons: An empty bag provides a comparison for whether the leaves made a difference.
The comparison does not test whether the plant has roots.
Neither bag measures a universal release rate.
Drops in one bag do not make drops in the other impossible.
plans.evidence: Comparing the leafy branch with an empty, equally dry bag also helps the observer decide whether the leaves made a difference.
plans.why: The text states the role of the comparison; the hypothetical result would weaken an explanation based only on the presence of leaves.
plans.method: Apply the stated purpose of a comparison to the possible observation named in the question.
plans.trap: An inference about a control should concern what the comparison can establish, not an unrelated plant fact.

passages.title: A Gap in the Ledger
passages.content:
The following is an original fictional account of a historical investigation.

When a town museum prepared a display about a fair held many years earlier, its volunteers found a ledger listing nine exhibitors. The list seemed complete: each name had a number beside it, and the final entry was followed by a heavy line. A volunteer drafted a label stating that exactly nine exhibitors had taken part. Before printing it, the group searched the museum’s box of old newspaper clippings.

One photograph showed a row of stalls at the fair. Most of the readable signs matched names in the ledger, but two signs did not. The volunteers could have added two to nine and announced a new total. Instead, they examined what the photograph actually established. A sign might belong to a second stall run by an exhibitor already listed. It might identify a sponsor rather than an exhibitor. The image raised a question; it did not answer every question.

The group compared the date on the clipping with the fair’s date and searched for an exhibitor map. No map appeared. A later letter mentioned an additional stall, but it did not explain who operated it. The museum therefore changed the display label to say that the surviving ledger listed nine exhibitors and might omit others. The volunteers left space beside it for the photograph.

The new label was less definite than the first draft, but it was more faithful to the records. Visitors could see both the ledger and the reason to doubt its completeness. The display presented historical inquiry as a process of weighing sources, rather than a contest to produce the boldest number.

plans.prompt: Why are the two unmatched signs an important detail?
choices: They cast doubt on the ledger’s completeness without proving an exact new total.
They prove that every ledger entry is false.
They establish that no fair took place.
They show that the museum volunteers wrote the ledger.
reasons: The signs create a specific uncertainty about what the list includes.
Most signs match ledger entries; the entire record is not disproved.
The image is evidence of stalls at the fair.
The ledger is an older record found by the volunteers.
plans.evidence: The image raised a question; it did not answer every question.
plans.why: The unmatched signs support doubt, but several possible explanations prevent an exact total.
plans.method: Connect the unmatched signs to the alternatives considered in the same paragraph.
plans.trap: Evidence of an incomplete record does not automatically reveal the missing total.

plans.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the investigation?
choices: The surviving records do not establish exactly how many exhibitors attended.
There were exactly eleven exhibitors.
The fair had no sponsors.
The ledger was deliberately falsified.
reasons: The volunteers preserve the known list while acknowledging unresolved omissions.
Two extra signs do not necessarily represent two extra exhibitors.
Sponsorship remains one possible explanation for a sign.
No motive or deliberate falsification is established.
plans.evidence: The museum therefore changed the display label to say that the surviving ledger listed nine exhibitors and might omit others.
plans.why: The label distinguishes what the ledger establishes from what the full attendance total might have been.
plans.method: Separate a documented count from the unknown complete count.
plans.trap: Do not assign a motive or exact total that the records do not establish.

plans.prompt: Why does the author describe the volunteers’ decision to revise the display label?
choices: To illustrate how historical claims should reflect both evidence and its limits.
To argue that museums should never display photographs.
To show that less definite statements are always incorrect.
To teach visitors how to organize a fair.
reasons: The revision makes the label more faithful to conflicting records.
The volunteers display the photograph as useful evidence.
The passage distinguishes certainty from accuracy rather than rejecting cautious statements.
The passage concerns interpreting records, not organizing an event.
plans.evidence: The new label was less definite than the first draft, but it was more faithful to the records.
plans.why: The author uses the revision to make a point about accurate, qualified historical interpretation.
plans.method: Identify the lesson the final comparison draws from the investigation.
plans.trap: The subject of a historical account is not necessarily the author’s instructional purpose.

plans.prompt: What is the function of “A sign might belong to a second stall run by an exhibitor already listed”?
choices: It gives an alternative explanation that limits the conclusion drawn from the photograph.
It proves which exhibitor owned the unmatched signs.
It introduces the museum’s final label as a direct quotation.
It explains how the volunteers repaired the ledger.
reasons: The possible shared ownership shows why signs cannot simply be counted as separate exhibitors.
The sentence offers a possibility, not proof of ownership.
The final label is described in a later paragraph.
No physical repair of the ledger occurs.
plans.evidence: A sign might belong to a second stall run by an exhibitor already listed.
plans.why: The possibility is used to challenge the simple addition of two signs to nine listed names.
plans.method: Ask what claim the sentence prevents readers from making too quickly.
plans.trap: A hypothetical explanation is not a confirmed event.

plans.prompt: How does finding the photograph change the course of the volunteers’ work?
choices: It turns a seemingly settled count into a question that requires further investigation.
It ends the investigation by establishing an exact total.
It causes the volunteers to abandon the display permanently.
It makes the letter unnecessary because the photograph names every exhibitor.
reasons: After the image, the volunteers inspect possible interpretations and seek more records.
The image does not resolve whether the signs represent separate exhibitors.
The museum completes a revised display.
The image does not identify every operator, and the volunteers still examine the letter.
plans.evidence: Instead, they examined what the photograph actually established.
plans.why: The photograph changes the task from repeating the ledger’s number to testing what the sources support.
plans.method: Compare the volunteers’ plan before the discovery with their actions afterward.
plans.trap: New evidence can increase uncertainty instead of closing an investigation.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Historical inquiry requires matching a conclusion to what the surviving records actually establish.
A photograph supplies a more precise fair-participation total than the surviving ledger.
A historical display is most useful when it presents a confident number instead of unresolved questions.
A surviving record loses its value once another source calls its completeness into question.
reasons: The revised label distinguishes the ledger’s known list from uncertainty about the fair’s complete participation.
The photograph raises doubt but its signs might identify sponsors or second stalls, so it does not establish a precise new total.
The display becomes more faithful by distinguishing what is known from what remains uncertain.
The ledger still establishes which names its surviving list includes; incomplete coverage does not make that information worthless.
plans.evidence: The museum therefore changed the display label to say that the surviving ledger listed nine exhibitors and might omit others.
plans.why: The revised label states the known list while retaining the uncertainty raised by other sources, showing why conclusions must match the evidence.
plans.method: Identify what the investigation teaches about the meaning and limits of its sources.
plans.trap: A record’s silence may reflect its purpose rather than prove that an event did not occur.

plans.prompt: What can be inferred about why the students examine more than one kind of record?
choices: Different records may preserve different aspects of the same event.
A later letter automatically supplies the correct total whenever older records disagree.
The volunteers need to choose one record and suppress conflicting evidence before displaying the fair’s history.
The heavy line beneath the ledger’s final entry is enough to dismiss the photograph’s unmatched signs.
reasons: The ledger lists names, the photograph shows signs, and the letter mentions a stall, so their information is complementary.
The letter mentions another stall but does not explain its operator, so later date alone does not make it a complete answer.
The final display presents both the ledger and the photograph, making the uncertainty available to visitors.
The apparent ending of the list motivates the first confident draft, but the other evidence still raises a valid question.
plans.evidence: The museum therefore changed the display label to say that the surviving ledger listed nine exhibitors and might omit others.
plans.why: The volunteers compare a ledger, a photograph, and a letter because each preserves a different piece of evidence and none establishes the full total alone.
plans.method: Connect the information each source preserves to the question the students are trying to answer.
plans.trap: Complementary evidence is useful even when no single source is complete.

passages.title: My First Route
passages.content:
I kept the folded transit map in my coat pocket long after I no longer needed it. On my first trip across the city alone, I had opened it at every stop. My aunt had drawn a small star beside the station where I needed to change trains. The map showed colored lines and neat dots; the station itself offered stairways, moving crowds, and announcements I could not quite hear. I missed my transfer because I was staring at the map instead of reading the sign above the platform.

At the next stop, I stepped aside and asked a station worker how to return. She did not grab the map from me. She asked me to find our current station, then to trace the line back one stop. As I did, the tangle of colors began to become a route. I rode back and made the transfer, arriving at my aunt’s apartment later than planned but without needing her to come for me.

For weeks afterward, I rehearsed the route in my mind before leaving home. Gradually, I stopped checking the map at familiar stops. I learned to look up from it, read the signs, and compare the real platform with the diagram. The map remained useful, but it stopped being a shield I held between myself and the station.

Years later, I found it while sorting the pockets of that old coat. The star was nearly rubbed away. I could have thrown the map out; a newer one was easier to read. Instead, I slipped it into a drawer. It reminded me of the worker’s patience and of a morning when asking for help had become part of learning to travel independently.

plans.prompt: Which statement best describes the narrator’s relationship to the events?
choices: The narrator recalls a personal experience and reflects on it from a later time.
The narrator reports events that happened only to a stranger.
The narrator knows the private thoughts of every person in the station.
The narrator describes the first trip while it is still happening.
reasons: First-person memories are followed by a scene years later.
The journey is repeatedly described as the narrator’s own.
The text reports actions and the narrator’s thoughts, not everyone’s thoughts.
The final paragraph establishes later reflection.
plans.evidence: Years later, I found it while sorting the pockets of that old coat.
plans.why: The narrator looks back across time rather than narrating solely from the moment of the first trip.
plans.method: Identify who uses “I” and look for time markers showing when the account is being remembered.
plans.trap: A first-person narrator does not automatically know other people’s private thoughts.

plans.prompt: How does the narrator change during the experience?
choices: The narrator learns to use the map together with observation and appropriate help.
The narrator stops using all transit information.
The narrator becomes certain that asking for help prevents independence.
The narrator decides never to travel alone again.
reasons: The narrator later combines the diagram with signs and remembers help as part of learning.
The map remains useful, and the narrator learns to read signs.
The final reflection directly connects help with independent travel.
The narrator continues using the route.
plans.evidence: I learned to look up from it, read the signs, and compare the real platform with the diagram.
plans.why: The narrator develops a more active way of navigating instead of relying on the diagram alone.
plans.method: Compare the first trip’s mistake with the later strategy the narrator learns.
plans.trap: Independence can include knowing when and how to ask for help.

plans.prompt: What does the saved map chiefly represent to the narrator?
choices: A remembered step toward independence and the help that made it possible.
The only reliable transit information available in the present.
A promise never to change trains.
Proof that the narrator’s aunt caused the missed transfer.
reasons: Its final value is connected to learning and the worker’s patience.
The narrator admits a newer map is easier to read.
The narrator successfully learns to make the transfer.
The passage does not blame the aunt.
plans.evidence: It reminded me of the worker’s patience and of a morning when asking for help had become part of learning to travel independently.
plans.why: The object carries the memory and meaning of a formative experience beyond its practical use.
plans.method: Distinguish why the object was first used from why it is kept years later.
plans.trap: A symbolic object can retain emotional meaning after its practical usefulness declines.

plans.prompt: What does the metaphor of the map as a “shield” suggest?
choices: The narrator had used the map to avoid engaging directly with the confusing station.
The map physically protected the narrator from falling objects.
The map made the station workers hostile.
The narrator believed the paper could stop the train.
reasons: The surrounding sentences contrast staring at the diagram with observing signs and the platform.
No physical danger or protective use is described.
The station worker is patient and helpful.
No such belief appears in the passage.
plans.evidence: The map remained useful, but it stopped being a shield I held between myself and the station.
plans.why: The shield metaphor characterizes the map as a way of avoiding the real surroundings, a habit the narrator overcomes.
plans.method: Connect the figurative comparison to the narrator’s changing behavior.
plans.trap: Do not read a figurative object as a literal physical tool.

plans.prompt: What perspective does the final paragraph add to the first journey?
choices: The later narrator values the lesson and patient help more than the embarrassment of arriving late.
The later narrator considers the journey entirely useless.
The later narrator still believes the old map is the best current guide.
The later narrator cannot remember who helped with the route.
reasons: The map is saved as a reminder of learning and patience.
The narrator gives the experience lasting significance.
A newer map is described as easier to read.
The worker’s help is explicitly remembered.
plans.evidence: Instead, I slipped it into a drawer.
plans.why: Choosing to keep the worn map after acknowledging a better one shows that its remembered meaning now matters most.
plans.method: Compare the immediate difficulty with what the older narrator chooses to remember and preserve.
plans.trap: A later perspective can change the significance of an earlier mistake.

plans.prompt: What is the main idea of this account?
choices: A worn map reminds the narrator that learning independence included looking closely and accepting help.
Following a transit map closely protects a traveler from needing to ask anyone for help.
A clearer replacement map removes the narrator’s reason to keep an older map.
Memorizing familiar routes makes signs in the real station unimportant.
reasons: The narrator learns to combine the diagram with real signs, accepts the worker’s guidance, and later keeps the map for that memory.
The first missed transfer and the worker’s guidance show that the map alone does not produce independence.
The narrator keeps the worn map for its memory of patient help, not because it is the clearest current tool.
The narrator explicitly learns to read signs and compare the platform with the diagram.
plans.evidence: It reminded me of the worker’s patience and of a morning when asking for help had become part of learning to travel independently.
plans.why: The closing reflection joins the practical lesson in navigation with the narrator’s recognition that accepting guidance can support independence.
plans.method: Connect the narrator’s starting expectations with the final understanding of the journey.
plans.trap: A main idea about a memoir should include what the experience comes to mean.

plans.prompt: Which conclusion about the narrator is most supported by the passage?
choices: The narrator’s understanding grows through direct experience, not only through a diagram of the route.
The worker’s help replaces the narrator’s need to interpret the map actively.
Independent travel requires the narrator to discard the old map and avoid guidance.
Years later, the old map’s main value is its greater practical accuracy than the newer one.
reasons: The narrator develops a perspective by combining the map with the actual journey.
The worker asks the narrator to find the station and trace a route rather than doing the interpretation for the narrator.
The account explicitly connects asking for help with learning independence, and the narrator retains the map.
The newer map is easier to read; the worn map’s retained value comes from the memory it carries.
plans.evidence: I learned to look up from it, read the signs, and compare the real platform with the diagram.
plans.why: The change in perspective connects concrete experience to an understanding not supplied by a diagram alone.
plans.method: Distinguish what the map supplies from what the narrator learns through the journey.
plans.trap: A supported inference should fit the whole development, not an extreme claim about every experience.

passages.title: What a Quiet Hour Changed
passages.content:
The events and interviews in this original news-style passage are fictional.

The Brook Street Library recently tested a quiet study hour after school. For one hour, a meeting room that usually hosted conversation was reserved for silent work. On the first afternoon, every chair was occupied. By the third afternoon, staff had added a waiting list. The librarian described the response as encouraging but said the trial would continue for two more weeks before the room’s regular schedule changed.

Students who attended said the room helped them concentrate. One student explained that the main reading area became noisy when classes arrived together. Another said that having a predictable quiet hour made it easier to plan a visit. Staff recorded the number of occupied chairs each day, but they did not compare participants’ grades or measure how much work they completed. High attendance showed demand for seats; it did not prove an improvement in academic performance.

A community chess group raised a different concern. Its members had previously used the meeting room at the same time. Moving their gathering to a smaller corner made conversation difficult, according to the group’s organizer. The librarian said a permanent schedule would need to account for both uses. A popular trial did not make the room unlimited.

Next week, the library plans to ask visitors which hours they can attend and whether an alternative room would serve either group. For now, the waiting list and the chess group’s concerns remain side by side in the staff’s notes. The decision will depend on more than which activity filled the room first.

plans.prompt: What does the librarian’s decision to continue the trial suggest?
choices: The librarian considers the early response useful but insufficient for a permanent decision.
The librarian believes the quiet hour has no users.
The librarian has already canceled every other room use.
The librarian knows that participants’ grades have improved.
reasons: The librarian delays a schedule change while gathering further information.
Every chair was occupied and a waiting list was added.
Both uses remain under consideration.
The staff did not measure grades.
plans.evidence: The librarian described the response as encouraging but said the trial would continue for two more weeks before the room’s regular schedule changed.
plans.why: The combination of encouragement and delay implies a cautious decision based on additional evidence.
plans.method: Infer the attitude shown by both the positive description and the postponed decision.
plans.trap: An encouraging trial is not the same as a completed decision.

plans.prompt: Which finding is actually supported by the waiting list?
choices: Demand for quiet-hour seats exceeded the available chairs.
Participants completed more schoolwork than all other library users.
Every neighborhood student preferred silent study.
The chess group no longer needed meeting space.
reasons: A waiting list means more people wanted seats than could be seated.
Work completion was not measured.
The waiting list does not represent every student.

passages.title: The Perfect Alarm
passages.content:
Mr. Vale called the new alarm perfect. It would record every opening of the library’s front door, he explained, so no one could enter unnoticed. Mara, who helped close the building each afternoon, asked whether the side window counted as a door. Mr. Vale smiled at what he took to be a joke and pointed again to the screen of neatly ordered times. Mara did not repeat the question.

The next morning, a small pot of basil had vanished from the reading-room sill. Nothing else seemed disturbed. Mr. Vale announced that the alarm log would identify the person who had taken it. Mara examined the sill instead. A crescent of damp soil lay beside a scuff on the paint, and the window’s latch rested open. Her friend Dev suggested searching the street immediately. Mara asked him to look for a smaller clue first: whether the soil continued onto the ledge outside. It did.

They went around the building and found the pot below the window, its rim chipped but the plant upright. Dev looked upward and noticed a pigeon landing on the outer ledge. The bird’s arrival did not prove exactly how the pot had fallen, but it made the open window worth considering. Mara carried the pot inside and showed Mr. Vale the unlatched frame.

The alarm had recorded no suspicious visit because the incident did not require anyone to use the front door. Mr. Vale read the log once more, as though another glance might widen what it measured. Then he shut the window and asked Mara to add the latch to the closing checklist. Her question had returned, this time without needing to be spoken. The perfect record had been complete only about the thing it recorded.

plans.prompt: What can the reader reasonably infer about Mara’s original question?
choices: She noticed a limitation in what the alarm could monitor.
She assumes the side window automatically triggers the alarm in the same way as the front door.
She asks the question mainly to embarrass Mr. Vale in front of the other workers.
She has decided that the log has no useful information before finding out what it measures.
reasons: Her question distinguishes the unmonitored window from the monitored door.
Her question tests the difference between openings instead of assuming the window is included.
The text shows her practical question but supplies no evidence of an intention to embarrass him.
Recognizing a possible limitation is different from rejecting useful front-door records altogether.
plans.evidence: Mara, who helped close the building each afternoon, asked whether the side window counted as a door.
plans.why: Her attention to the window suggests she recognizes that recording door openings does not cover every possible event.
plans.method: Connect Mara’s question to the later discovery of the open latch, without adding knowledge she could not yet have.
plans.trap: A reasonable inference differs from an invented prediction.

plans.prompt: Which trait does Mara most clearly demonstrate during the search?
choices: Careful attention to what evidence can actually establish.
A desire to accuse the first person she meets.
Indifference to whether the plant is recovered.
Unquestioning trust in an impressive new device.
reasons: She follows the soil and considers the window while limiting the conclusion about the bird.
Mara does not identify or accuse a person.
She searches and carries the pot back inside.
She questions the alarm’s coverage from the beginning.
plans.evidence: The bird’s arrival did not prove exactly how the pot had fallen, but it made the open window worth considering.
plans.why: The narration models the same caution Mara’s investigation shows: consider a clue without treating a possibility as proof.
plans.method: Identify a repeated pattern in the character’s actions rather than a single object she notices.
plans.trap: Finding a possible explanation does not justify claiming certainty.

plans.prompt: Which event most directly brings about a change in the closing routine?
choices: Mara returns the pot and shows Mr.Vale the open window latch.
Mr.Vale first describes the alarm as perfect.
Dev proposes searching the street.
A list of times appears on the alarm screen.
reasons: Showing the unlatched window leads Mr.Vale to add it to the checklist.
The first description does not change the routine.

plans.evidence: Then he shut the window and asked Mara to add the latch to the closing checklist.
plans.why: The displayed limitation of the alarm produces the concrete change that resolves the practical problem.
plans.method: Trace which discovery leads directly to the corrective action at the end.
plans.trap: An event that starts a story need not be the event that resolves its problem.

plans.prompt: What underlying conflict does the incident expose?
choices: The difference between Mr.Vale’s confidence in the alarm and the limited range of events it records.
A competition between Mara and Dev to own the plant.
A disagreement about whether plants belong in libraries.
A battle between two library departments over their opening hours.
reasons: The device’s perfect log fails to explain an incident outside its coverage.
Neither friend claims ownership of the pot.
No objection to plants is described.
No departmental scheduling dispute appears.
plans.evidence: The perfect record had been complete only about the thing it recorded.
plans.why: The ending states the tension between an accurate measurement and an overly broad belief about what it proves.
plans.method: Distinguish the immediate missing-pot problem from the mistaken assumption the incident challenges.
plans.trap: A conflict may concern competing understandings rather than a quarrel.

plans.prompt: Why is the title “The Perfect Alarm” ironic?
choices: The alarm works as designed but cannot explain the very incident its owner expects it to solve.
The alarm secretly records conversations instead of door openings.

reasons: The owner’s broad expectation conflicts with the device’s narrow, functioning measurement.
No recording of conversations is described.
The log has no information about birds.
Mara does not damage the device.
plans.evidence: The alarm had recorded no suspicious visit because the incident did not require anyone to use the front door.
plans.why: The mismatch between the claim of perfection and the actual usefulness of the record creates situational irony.
plans.method: Compare what the title and owner lead readers to expect with what the incident reveals.
plans.trap: Irony is an expectation–outcome contrast, not merely any surprising detail.

plans.prompt: How does the relationship between Mara and Mr.Vale change by the end?
choices: He moves from dismissing her question to asking her to improve the procedure.
She stops helping at the library because he refuses to listen.
He gives her sole responsibility for designing an alarm.
She agrees that his first explanation covered every possible event.
reasons: He initially treats the question as a joke, then accepts her evidence and asks for a checklist change.
She remains involved in the closing routine.
The request concerns a latch checklist, not designing an alarm.
The ending exposes the limitation of his first claim.
plans.evidence: Mr. Vale smiled at what he took to be a joke and pointed again to the screen of neatly ordered times.
plans.why: This early dismissal contrasts with his later request that Mara add the latch to the checklist, showing increased respect for her practical observation.
plans.method: Compare how one character responds to the other’s contribution at the beginning and at the end.
plans.trap: A change in respect need not be announced directly.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: A careful investigation reveals that a precise door record cannot explain every incident in the library.
The alarm is valuable only if it replaces front-door monitoring with window monitoring.
Mara restores Mr. Vale’s confidence in the log by identifying a visitor responsible for the missing pot.

reasons: Mara follows soil and the window latch to locate the pot, exposing the limited scope of the supposedly perfect alarm.
The lesson concerns the scope of a useful measurement, not abandoning door monitoring for a different narrow measurement.
No suspicious front-door visit is needed to explain the incident, and the exact cause remains unproved.
Mara follows physical clues carefully; the story does not establish a guilty person or make blame its solution.
plans.evidence: The perfect record had been complete only about the thing it recorded.
plans.why: The final qualification ties the investigation to the broader lesson about interpreting an accurate record within its scope.
plans.method: Trace what the passage develops from the opening through its outcome or concluding interpretation.
plans.trap: A main idea accounts for the passage’s development and preserves its limits; one striking detail is not enough.

passages.title: Room for the Box
passages.content:
The ferry’s upper deck had one empty bench when Tomas and his sister June reached it. Tomas set their wooden box on the seat and leaned against the rail, relieved that they would not have to hold it for the whole crossing. Inside were the paper scenery pieces for their school play. A sharp bend would leave a white scar across the painted night sky, and they had already repaired it twice.

A woman carrying a sleepy child came up the stairs and stopped beside the bench. Tomas looked from the child to the box. He imagined reaching school with crushed scenery and facing the classmates who had painted it. June picked the box up before he spoke. She balanced it on her knees and motioned for the woman to sit. Tomas wanted to tell her that she was risking everyone’s work. Instead, he took the opposite end of the box so it would not sag.

Halfway across, a gust lifted one loose strip from the box. Tomas caught it against his coat. June shifted her grip, and together they slid the lid into place. The woman held her child with one arm and steadied the lid with her other hand. For the rest of the crossing, the box traveled with three pairs of hands around it.

At the landing, Tomas checked the painted sky. Its stars were uncreased. The woman thanked them, but June only asked whether she needed help with the stairs. Tomas carried the box below, turning sideways to leave room for the child. He had pictured kindness as something that would cost them the scenery. The crossing had shown him another possibility: protecting the work and making space for someone could be parts of the same task.

plans.prompt: Which theme is most fully developed by the passage?
choices: Cooperation can make room for kindness without abandoning responsibility.
Valuable work can be protected only by refusing to help others.
Younger siblings always make better decisions than older siblings.
A difficult journey always destroys carefully prepared work.
reasons: The siblings and passenger cooperate to protect the scenery while sharing the bench.
The work arrives intact after they help the passenger.
The passage presents one sibling interaction, not a universal age rule.
The scenery survives the crossing.
plans.evidence: The crossing had shown him another possibility: protecting the work and making space for someone could be parts of the same task.
plans.why: The final reflection connects the practical result to a general insight about kindness and responsibility.
plans.method: Relate the characters’ decision and its outcome to a general idea that extends beyond the ferry.
plans.trap: A theme should not be a universal claim that the story’s details cannot support.

plans.prompt: Which sentence could replace the description of the scenery’s fragility with a simile that preserves the stated meaning?
choices: The painted sky was as easy to crease as a thin sheet of paper.
The painted sky was as heavy as the ferry’s anchor.
The painted sky was like a lamp that made its own light.
The painted sky was as rigid as the steel rail.
reasons: The comparison explicitly conveys the scenery’s vulnerability to bending.
The passage is concerned with fragility, not extreme weight.
Nothing suggests the scenery produces light.
Rigidity contradicts the stated risk of creasing.
plans.evidence: A sharp bend would leave a white scar across the painted night sky, and they had already repaired it twice.
plans.why: A simile comparing the scenery to easily creased paper preserves the physical vulnerability the sentence describes.
plans.method: Identify the quality being emphasized, then choose a comparison using “like” or “as” that expresses that quality.
plans.trap: A simile must fit the relevant quality, not merely share a word with the passage.

plans.prompt: Which summary best preserves the passage’s central sequence?
choices: Tomas worries that sharing a bench will damage the scenery, but cooperation protects it and changes his view of helping.
June drops the box, the scenery is destroyed, and Tomas refuses to help the passenger.
A passenger paints a new sky for the siblings, who then leave their play behind.
Tomas rides the ferry alone and discovers that its benches need repair.
reasons: This includes the concern, cooperative response, outcome, and changed understanding.
The scenery remains intact, and Tomas joins the effort.
No new scenery is painted and the play is not abandoned.
June and the passenger are central to the events.
plans.evidence: At the landing, Tomas checked the painted sky. Its stars were uncreased.
plans.why: The intact scenery is the outcome that allows Tomas to reconsider the supposed conflict between helping and protecting the work.
plans.method: Retain the initiating concern, decisive action, and important result while omitting incidental details.
plans.trap: A summary should preserve the story’s causal sequence, not collect colorful objects.

plans.prompt: What does the phrase “a white scar across the painted night sky” emphasize?
choices: A crease would leave a lasting, visible mark on the scenery.
A real storm is approaching the ferry.
The scenery can heal itself like a living body.
Tomas has injured his arm while painting.
reasons: Calling the crease a scar emphasizes a visible mark that repairs may not fully conceal.
The phrase refers to painted paper, not actual weather.
The comparison does not give the paper a literal ability to heal.
No bodily injury is described.
plans.evidence: A sharp bend would leave a white scar across the painted night sky, and they had already repaired it twice.
plans.why: The figurative word “scar” gives the possible crease a sense of lasting damage.
plans.method: Translate the figurative description back into the actual object and identify the quality it highlights.
plans.trap: A metaphor transfers a quality; it does not turn the object into the thing compared.

plans.prompt: How does the passage’s point of view shape the reader’s understanding?
choices: It reveals Tomas’s fears and later reflection while showing the other characters mainly through their actions.
It reveals every passenger’s private thoughts equally.
It presents only June’s first-person account.
It offers an impersonal report with no access to any character’s thoughts.
reasons: The narration describes Tomas’s imagined failure and his changed understanding.
The passenger’s and June’s private thoughts are not reported.
The account uses third person and centers Tomas’s perspective.
The narration explicitly gives Tomas’s worries and reflection.
plans.evidence: He imagined reaching school with crushed scenery and facing the classmates who had painted it.
plans.why: Access to this private imagined outcome establishes the focus on Tomas’s interior perspective.
plans.method: Identify whose unspoken thoughts the narration presents and distinguish them from observable actions.
plans.trap: Third-person narration can remain limited to one character’s perspective.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the passage’s main idea?
choices: Tomas discovers that helping another passenger can be compatible with protecting the scenery he is responsible for.
Tomas decides that scenery is safest only when it occupies a passenger’s seat.
June persuades Tomas that protecting the class’s work deserves less attention than the passengers’ comfort.
The crossing teaches Tomas that helping a passenger is worthwhile chiefly when that passenger returns a favor.
reasons: The shared effort keeps the box intact while making space for the woman and child.
The box remains intact while being held cooperatively, so the outcome challenges the initial need to keep the seat for it.
June keeps protecting the scenery while making room; the final lesson joins rather than ranks the two responsibilities.
The woman helps with the lid, but the siblings offer the seat before any promised exchange or expectation of reward.
plans.evidence: protecting the work and making space for someone could be parts of the same task.
plans.why: Tomas’s final understanding connects the intact scenery and the assistance he gives, rather than treating responsibility and generosity as opposites.
plans.method: Trace what the passage develops from the opening through its outcome or concluding interpretation.
plans.trap: A main idea accounts for the passage’s development and preserves its limits; one striking detail is not enough.

plans.prompt: What can be inferred from Tomas taking the opposite end of the box after June lifts it?
choices: Despite his concern, he cooperates with her choice to make room for the woman.
He accepts June’s plan because he is certain from the beginning that the scenery will stay intact.
He tries to make June protect the box alone while he concentrates on making room on the bench.
He takes the box in order to stop June from sharing the bench with the woman.
reasons: His action supports the box even though he initially worries about June’s decision.
His imagined crushed scenery and concern about classmates show uncertainty, even though he cooperates.
Taking the opposite end shares the protective work instead of leaving it to June alone.
The action supports June’s decision and allows the woman to sit rather than preventing it.
plans.evidence: Instead, he took the opposite end of the box so it would not sag.
plans.why: The sentence directly states the practical action; his cooperation with June’s decision follows from the contrast with what he wanted to say.
plans.method: Connect the exact clue to its surrounding actions or argument; distinguish what is stated from the conclusion it supports.
plans.trap: A defensible inference follows from the text without adding an unsupported motive, guarantee, or universal claim.

passages.title: The Roof at Dawn
passages.content:
Before the buses wake,
the roof keeps last night’s rain
in shallow cups of silver.
A bent antenna points
to somewhere past the clouds,
though nothing follows it.

Below, a shutter rattles up.
The bakery breathes warm air
through a narrow open door.
Its light lays one gold ribbon
across the empty sidewalk;
a pigeon steps around it.

I used to think the morning
arrived in one great sweep,
a curtain pulled aside.
But here it comes in pieces:
a key, a wheel, a lifted lid,
a hand that sets out bread.

The puddles hold the sky
until the first shoes stir them.
Their small bright maps dissolve.
No trumpet marks the moment.
The street becomes itself
by people doing ordinary things.

plans.prompt: How does “The bakery breathes warm air” use personification?
choices: It describes the building’s release of warm air as a living creature’s breath.
It claims that bread is literally alive.
It compares the bakery to a metal tool.
It gives a detailed scientific account of human breathing.
reasons: The nonhuman bakery is assigned the animate action of breathing.
The personification concerns the bakery and warm air, not living bread.
No tool comparison appears.
The line is a figurative description rather than a physiological explanation.
plans.evidence: The bakery breathes warm air
plans.why: The verb gives the awakening street a sense of life through an ordinary physical detail.
plans.method: Identify the nonhuman subject and the human or animal action attributed to it.
plans.trap: Personification is an assigned living action or quality, not every vivid description.

plans.prompt: What does the image of “one gold ribbon” across the sidewalk help the reader visualize?
choices: A narrow band of warm light spreading from the bakery door.
A fabric ribbon that the pigeon carries away.
A painted line being added to the street.
The whole sky turning completely dark.
reasons: The preceding reference to the bakery’s light identifies the ribbon as light.
The pigeon steps around the image; no fabric is carried.
No painting activity is described.
The image belongs to dawn’s growing light.
plans.evidence:
Its light lays one gold ribbon
across the empty sidewalk;
plans.why: Color and shape turn the patch of light into a clear visual image.
plans.method: Read the image with its grammatical subject to identify what produces the imagined shape.
plans.trap: A concrete image can describe light without introducing a literal object.

plans.prompt: Which mood is created by the poem’s attention to quiet, ordinary actions?
choices: Reflective calm.
Urgent terror.
Bitter hostility.
Triumphant celebration of a victory.
reasons: Small details, patient observation, and the absence of a trumpet create a quiet contemplative feeling.
There is no threat or emergency.
The speaker shows no resentment toward the people described.
The ending emphasizes ordinary activity rather than a victory.
plans.evidence: No trumpet marks the moment.
plans.why: The rejection of a grand announcement supports the calm mood of gradual, ordinary awakening.
plans.method: Connect the pace, sensory details, and scale of the actions to the feeling they create for the reader.
plans.trap: Mood concerns the atmosphere created for the reader, not merely the time of day.

plans.prompt: Why is “pieces” effective in “But here it comes in pieces”?
choices: It emphasizes that morning becomes noticeable through many separate small actions.
It suggests that the speaker wants to break the street apart.
It proves that daylight arrives only on this roof.
It refers only to the pieces of bread inside the bakery.
reasons: The following list of a key, wheel, lid, and hand develops the idea of many small contributions.
The poem observes activity without proposing destruction.
No exclusive claim about this roof is made.
Bread is one detail among several, not the whole referent.
plans.evidence:
But here it comes in pieces:
a key, a wheel, a lifted lid,
a hand that sets out bread.
plans.why: The word counters the earlier expectation of a single dramatic arrival with an accumulation of ordinary details.
plans.method: Compare the word with the expectation stated in the preceding lines and the examples that follow.
plans.trap: A word’s effect depends on its contrast and examples, not only its dictionary meaning.

plans.prompt: Which description best captures the speaker’s tone toward the street’s morning activity?
choices: Appreciative and observant.
Mocking and dismissive.
Accusatory and distrustful.
Confused about whether dawn exists.
reasons: The speaker notices ordinary work carefully and finds meaning in its gradual contribution.
The details are valued, not mocked.
No wrongdoing is alleged.
The speaker revises an expectation about how dawn feels, not its existence.
plans.evidence:
The street becomes itself
by people doing ordinary things.
plans.why: The ending gives ordinary actions a constructive significance, revealing appreciation rather than dismissal.
plans.method: Ask how the speaker evaluates the subject, using the ending and selected details.
plans.trap: Tone is the speaker’s attitude; it is related to but distinct from the reader’s mood.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the poem’s central idea?
choices: Morning becomes meaningful through the accumulation of ordinary human activities.
Morning loses its beauty as workers disturb the patterns left by the night’s rain.
Quiet natural details matter more to the street’s identity than the people who work there.
The street becomes itself through a single dramatic transformation at daybreak.
reasons: The list of keys, wheels, lids, and bread builds to the claim that ordinary actions make the street itself.
The puddle images change, but the appreciative ending values the ordinary actions that animate the street.
The final lines give people’s ordinary activities a central role, not a lesser role than weather.
The speaker explicitly revises the expectation of one great sweep in favor of separate small beginnings.
plans.evidence:
The street becomes itself
by people doing ordinary things.
plans.why: The ending synthesizes the separate observations into an understanding of a place made active by daily work.
plans.method: Trace what the passage develops from the opening through its outcome or concluding interpretation.
plans.trap: A main idea accounts for the passage’s development and preserves its limits; one striking detail is not enough.

plans.prompt: What can be inferred about how the speaker’s understanding of morning has changed?
choices: The speaker now notices many small beginnings rather than expecting one dramatic arrival.
The speaker withdraws from the street’s activity to value only the separate world of the roof.
The speaker is disappointed that ordinary actions fail to create the dramatic arrival once expected.
The speaker now explains the street’s morning mainly through changes in weather rather than work.
reasons: The poem contrasts the former idea of one great sweep with a key, wheel, lid, and hand.
The poem looks from the roof to the bakery and street, joining the observations rather than rejecting the activity below.
The ending finds meaning in ordinary actions; it does not express disappointment in their scale.
Rain and reflected sky form images, but keys, wheels, lids, and bread develop the change in understanding.
plans.evidence:
But here it comes in pieces:
a key, a wheel, a lifted lid,
a hand that sets out bread.
plans.why: The contrast with “I used to think” supports a shift in perspective toward gradual, ordinary contributions.
plans.method: Connect the exact clue to its surrounding actions or argument; distinguish what is stated from the conclusion it supports.
plans.trap: A defensible inference follows from the text without adding an unsupported motive, guarantee, or universal claim.

passages.title: The Importance of a Second Calculation
passages.content:
Katherine Johnson’s work at the agency that became NASA joined mathematical skill to a practical question: how could a spacecraft reach a chosen destination? A trajectory calculation had to connect a path through space with the conditions of launch and landing. The problem was not solved merely by producing a page of numbers. Those numbers had to describe the mission’s intended course.

In 1960, Johnson and engineer Ted Skopinski coauthored a report on the equations for an orbital flight with a specified landing position. Johnson also performed trajectory analysis for Alan Shepard’s 1961 mission. These tasks placed her work directly within the decisions that shaped early American human spaceflight. They illustrate a connection between mathematical research and the operational needs of a mission.

When NASA prepared for John Glenn’s orbital flight in 1962, electronic computers were already central to the calculations. Glenn nevertheless asked Johnson to check the computer’s trajectory figures. The request did not mean that all electronic computation was useless. It showed the value placed on an additional check by a mathematician whose judgment the astronaut trusted.

A second calculation can serve a different purpose from the first. Rather than replacing every tool, it tests whether the result is dependable enough for the decision at hand. In Johnson’s case, mathematical expertise mattered alongside the growing speed of electronic machines. Her role challenges a simple story in which a newer technology immediately makes earlier skills irrelevant. The machines changed how work could be done; the need to understand and verify their output remained.

plans.prompt: How does the author develop Johnson’s role in the passage?
choices: By connecting examples of her calculations to mission planning and trusted verification.
By listing only honors that she received after retirement.
By describing her as an opponent of every electronic computer.
By explaining that her work had no practical use.
reasons: The report, Shepard analysis, and Glenn check all relate mathematical work to mission needs.
No retirement honors are listed.

passages.title: A Bench We Can Change
passages.content:
The following is an original fictional speech to a school council.

Members of the council, we should test a movable bench near the courtyard’s eastern wall before spending our full budget on a permanent seating area. Students have asked for somewhere to sit outside, and that request deserves a response. But a useful response must answer more than whether we can buy a bench. It must tell us whether the location serves the people who need it and whether it leaves enough room for other activities.

Some members argue that a permanent bench would show that we take the request seriously. They worry that a trial will look like another postponement. That is a reasonable concern, especially for students who have waited through several meetings. A trial without a deadline could indeed become an excuse to do nothing. I propose something different: a four-week test, a public schedule for collecting comments, and a decision at the next council meeting.

During the test, we should record how the bench is used at different times, not simply count seats filled on one sunny afternoon. We should ask the students who use mobility devices whether the route remains clear. We should also hear from the classes that use the courtyard for demonstrations. Their needs may not appear in a simple count of people sitting down.

A trial will not reveal every possible future problem. It can, however, expose difficulties while we can still move the bench. If the location works, the observations will support a permanent plan. If it does not, a changeable design will let us respond without undoing an expensive installation. Testing is therefore a way to make our commitment more responsible, provided we also commit to an actual decision. Let us offer students a place to sit and give ourselves a way to learn where that place should be.

passages.title: Instructions for the Next Crew
passages.content:
The following is an original work of science fiction; its invented technology is part of the story.

Log for the next crew: the greenhouse screen will report that every tray is healthy. Do not mistake this sentence for an instruction to discard the screen. It measures water, light, and temperature more steadily than we can. But last week, when the vines filled the upper frame, it continued to report the same good numbers while the oldest leaves crowded the new ones out of the light. The screen measures light above each tray, not light reaching every leaf.

At first, Ren wanted to increase the lamps’ output. I wanted to remove the tallest vines. Both plans would have changed the whole tray to solve a problem affecting only part of it. We postponed either change long enough to trace the shadows through one full lamp cycle. That patient delay felt harder than pressing a bright, decisive button. By the end of the cycle, however, we could see where the adjustable supports had tilted inward.

Ren had been in charge of checking the supports when we arrived. I could have written that fact in this log as an accusation. Instead, I recorded the hinge’s gradual movement. A loose fitting could pass a quick inspection and shift later under the vines’ weight. Ren moved one support and watched the shadow thin. We changed the fitting, then recorded both the repair and the screen’s limitation.

Future crews will still use the numbers. They should also compare those numbers with the living arrangement beneath the sensor. A useful report can be accurate and incomplete at the same time. If this log sounds cautious, that is because we learned that the quickest-looking repair may begin by answering the wrong question. We leave you healthy trays and, more importantly, a reason to keep looking at them.

passages.title: Two Ways to Remember a Square
passages.content:
The following paired passages present fictional writers’ arguments about the same public square.

TextA: A Square Made Legible

Our square has changed names twice, and its oldest pavement lies beneath the newer stone. A visitor can cross it every day without learning either fact. I favor small signs that explain those changes. A sign cannot contain the whole history, but it can turn an unnoticed feature into a question a person might pursue. The old curb exposed by a repair becomes more than an inconvenient ridge when a reader learns why it is there.

Critics fear that signs will make the square feel like a museum. That danger depends partly on the kind of signs we choose. A commanding panel that tells visitors what to think would interrupt the place; a brief account with a source and an open question could invite attention. Legibility need not mean a final interpretation. It can give people a starting point while leaving them room to disagree.

TextB: A Square Kept in Conversation

I also want visitors to learn the square’s past. Yet I hesitate to place that work entirely in fixed signs. A permanent label acquires an authority that its small size rarely deserves. Which version of a contested event gets the wall, and which becomes a footnote? Even a label written with care can make one account look like the place’s settled voice.

I would begin with recorded conversations from residents and rotating outdoor readings. These would not be complete either; some voices would still be missing, and organizing the events would take work. Their advantage is that they can make differences of memory audible. Rather than remove every sign, I would ask that any sign identify its limits and point visitors toward those continuing conversations. The square should be a place where history is encountered and questioned, not merely received.

plans.why: B’s qualified acceptance of signs distinguishes the actual contrast from a simple for-or-against-signs division.
plans.method: State each proposal with its qualifications before comparing them.
plans.trap: A comparison can be wrong by exaggerating one side’s position.
