plans.method: Trace what the passage develops from the opening through its outcome or concluding interpretation.
plans.trap: A main idea accounts for the passage’s development and preserves its limits; one striking detail is not enough.

plans.prompt: How would B most likely respond to a proposed sign that identifies its sources and directs visitors to recorded conversations about conflicting memories?
choices: B would likely support its limited role as a connection to continuing inquiry, while resisting treating it as the square’s final account.
B would reject it simply because every written sign prevents residents from sharing memories.
B would support it only if it replaced outdoor readings and settled the conflicting accounts.
B would reject its references to conflicting memories because disagreement makes the square’s history unusable.
reasons: B permits signs that identify limits and point toward continuing conversations; the proposed sign serves that qualified role.
B explicitly says not to remove every sign, so a categorical rejection is unsupported.
B values ongoing conversations and audible differences rather than their replacement by a settled account.
B presents differences of memory as an advantage, not a reason to make history unusable.
plans.evidence: Rather than remove every sign, I would ask that any sign identify its limits and point visitors toward those continuing conversations.
plans.why: The sentence directly states the conditions for a useful sign. Applying those conditions to the proposed source-aware, conversation-linked sign supports the predicted response without inventing a categorical ban.
plans.method: Connect the exact clue to its surrounding actions or argument; distinguish what is stated from the conclusion it supports.
plans.trap: A defensible inference follows from the text without adding an unsupported motive, guarantee, or universal claim.

passages.title: The Map with a Blank
passages.content:
In a city that kept its stories on copper sheets, the mapmaker was asked to finish a map of the forest. Every road had to reach an edge, every stream had to find a river, and no space was to remain unmarked. The council promised a silver pen to whoever could complete the work. Three mapmakers drew paths where travelers disagreed, but the paths joined so elegantly that the council praised them before anyone walked them.

The youngest mapmaker, Sen, returned with a blank at the forest’s center. The council frowned. Sen explained that the paths there shifted when the river flooded, and no two travelers had followed the same crossing. The blank did not mean that nothing existed. It meant that Sen did not yet know which lines could be trusted. The council replied that uncertainty was what the silver pen had been offered to erase.

Sen took the unfinished map to the forest. At the first fork, a traveler asked why the blank had not been filled. Sen handed over the pen and asked him to draw the route he knew. A second traveler added a different route, and a third marked where water had covered a crossing. Sen wrote dates beside their lines. The map grew crowded at its center, yet its margins remained precise.

When Sen brought it back, the council said it was harder to read than the elegant maps. Sen agreed. Then she asked which map they would carry when the water rose. The council sent a messenger with each version. Only the messenger carrying Sen’s map knew where another traveler had reported a flooded crossing.

The council never declared Sen’s map complete. It hung the silver pen beside the blank spaces and invited each returning traveler to add a dated line. The forest did not become simpler. The map became more honest about what a traveler would have to decide.

plans.prompt: Which theme is developed by the council’s changed use of the silver pen?
choices: Acknowledging uncertainty can make knowledge more useful than pretending it is complete.
A beautiful diagram is always more dependable than observed experience.
People should refuse to share knowledge unless they know everything.
A map becomes honest only when all its details are erased.
reasons: The pen shifts from rewarding false completeness to inviting dated contributions.
The elegant maps fail to identify a reported flooded crossing.
Sen invites travelers to share partial knowledge.
The map keeps precise margins and adds dated details rather than erasing everything.
plans.evidence: The forest did not become simpler. The map became more honest about what a traveler would have to decide.
plans.why: The ending values informed decisions based on acknowledged limits rather than an artificially simplified picture.
plans.method: Trace how an object’s purpose changes and connect that change to the story’s final contrast.
plans.trap: Admitting uncertainty is not the same as rejecting all knowledge.

plans.prompt: What does the blank space most strongly symbolize?
choices: An acknowledged limit in the mapmaker’s knowledge that invites further inquiry.
A forest area known to contain nothing at all.
A punishment for travelers who disagree.
A command that the river stop flooding.
reasons: Sen explains that the blank marks uncertainty about trustworthy routes and later uses it to gather reports.
The passage explicitly says it does not mean nothing exists.
Disagreement is used as information rather than punished.
The map does not control the river.
plans.evidence: The blank did not mean that nothing existed. It meant that Sen did not yet know which lines could be trusted.
plans.why: The space represents the boundary between what is observed and what has not yet been established.
plans.method: Use the character’s explanation of the object and its later role to infer its symbolic meaning.
plans.trap: An absence on a representation does not necessarily signify an absence in the represented world.

plans.prompt: What is ironic about the council’s initial praise of the elegant maps?
choices: The maps seem complete before testing, but their neatness hides missing knowledge that matters during travel.
The council knows the elegant maps are accurate and falsely claims they are incomplete.
The travelers prefer an empty map because they never enter the forest.
The silver pen cannot make any mark on paper.
reasons: The apparent strength of clean completeness becomes a weakness compared with dated reports of a flood.
The council praises them before anyone walks their paths.
Travelers enter the forest and provide routes.
The pen is used to add travelers’ lines.
plans.evidence: the council praised them before anyone walked them.
plans.why: Approval rests on appearance before verification, so the later test reverses the expected advantage of the elegant maps.
plans.method: Compare the grounds for early approval with the result of the later practical test.
plans.trap: Irony depends on an expectation that the outcome qualifies or reverses.

plans.prompt: What is the function of the paragraph in which Sen asks travelers to draw their routes?
choices: It turns an admitted gap into a process for gathering and qualifying new information.
It proves that every traveler’s memory is identical.
It ends the problem by making the map permanently complete.
It explains how the council manufactures silver.
reasons: The travelers contribute differing routes and dated flood observations.
Their accounts differ and are recorded separately.
The council never declares the map complete.
No manufacturing process is described.
plans.evidence: Sen wrote dates beside their lines.
plans.why: Dating the different accounts preserves when each observation applied, making the map a developing record rather than a false final answer.
plans.method: Identify how the paragraph changes the meaning and use of the original problem.
plans.trap: Gathering more information does not automatically settle every uncertainty.

plans.prompt: Why does “elegantly” have a more doubtful connotation after the story’s practical test?
choices: The attractive appearance of the lines contrasts with the untested knowledge behind them.
The word comes to mean that the copper sheets are very heavy.
The word proves that all artistic skill is harmful.
The word reveals that the mapmakers intentionally caused the flood.
reasons: The story separates pleasing design from verified usefulness.
The physical weight of copper is not relevant to the change in meaning.
The criticism concerns untested claims, not all artistry.
No person causes the river’s flooding.
plans.evidence: the paths joined so elegantly that the council praised them before anyone walked them.
plans.why: The initial positive association of elegance becomes qualified when readers see that neatly joined paths can conceal unsupported choices.
plans.method: Reconsider the descriptive word in light of what the later events reveal about the praised object.
plans.trap: A changed connotation can qualify praise without reversing the word’s literal meaning.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the passage’s central idea?
choices: A developing map that acknowledges uncertain knowledge can become more useful than a neat map pretending to be complete.
Sen discovers that gathering travelers’ reports makes every forest route permanently unchanging.
The council learns that a pleasing appearance guarantees a route’s safety.
Sen abandons every reliable line because some crossings are uncertain.
reasons: Dated contributions preserve differing observations, and the practical test exposes an omission in the elegant maps.
Floods change crossings, and the council never declares the map complete.
The praised elegant maps omit a reported flooded crossing.
The margins remain precise, so known information is retained alongside acknowledged uncertainty.
plans.evidence: The forest did not become simpler. The map became more honest about what a traveler would have to decide.
plans.why: The final contrast shows usefulness arising from qualified knowledge rather than a simplified appearance that conceals decisions travelers still face.
plans.method: Trace what the passage develops from the opening through its outcome or concluding interpretation.
plans.trap: A main idea accounts for the passage’s development and preserves its limits; one striking detail is not enough.

plans.prompt: What can be inferred about the council’s changed decision to hang the silver pen beside the blank spaces?
choices: It now treats incomplete knowledge as an invitation to continuing contributions rather than merely a defect to erase.
It now forbids travelers from changing any mark on the map.
It has proved that all travelers followed identical crossings.
It has decided that no part of the forest can ever be mapped.
reasons: The pen once rewarded completion but now invites dated additions from returning travelers.
The council explicitly invites each traveler to add a line.
The earlier accounts differed and the river’s crossings changed.
The map retains precise margins and gains additional route information.
plans.evidence: It hung the silver pen beside the blank spaces and invited each returning traveler to add a dated line.
plans.why: The new use of the same reward object supports a changed view of uncertainty as a continuing task, not something to hide behind invented lines.
plans.method: Connect the exact clue to its surrounding actions or argument; distinguish what is stated from the conclusion it supports.
plans.trap: A defensible inference follows from the text without adding an unsupported motive, guarantee, or universal claim.

passages.title: A Different Ending
passages.content:
Aya had learned every word of her part before the first rehearsal. At home, she had stood beside the kitchen table and spoken each line loudly enough for her brother to hear from the hall. She imagined the audience leaning forward whenever she began to speak. On the school stage, however, her loudest line made her partner lose his place.

“You started before I finished,” Luis said. He pointed to a line in his script. “My character is still asking the question.”

Aya looked at her own page. The words she had memorized were all there. She had not practiced the silence before them. The director asked the pair to try the scene again, this time letting Luis finish. Aya waited, but the pause felt so long that she rushed her answer. Luis smiled at a moment when his character was supposed to be worried. The scene sounded like a disagreement about homework instead of an invitation to an adventure.

They took their scripts to the empty cafeteria during the break. Luis read his line quietly. Aya listened for the question rather than for her own turn. When he stopped, she looked at him for a moment before answering. He set his script down. “That sounded as if you really had to decide,” he said.

At the next rehearsal, Aya marked a small pause in the margin of her page. She still spoke clearly, but she no longer tried to make every line the loudest in the room. The director asked them to repeat the ending once more and invited the rest of the cast to watch. Aya noticed that several students leaned forward before she spoke. For the first time, she understood that the silence could be part of her work too.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Aya learns that listening and timing can make her acting more effective.
Aya decides that a performer should never speak loudly.
Luis persuades Aya to give up her part in the play.
Aya learns the words of her part for the first time at school.
reasons: The rehearsal improves when she listens to Luis and uses the pause intentionally.
She continues to speak clearly; the problem is making every line the loudest.
She keeps her role and improves the scene with Luis.
The first sentence says she learned every word before rehearsal.
plans.evidence: For the first time, she understood that the silence could be part of her work too.
plans.why: The final realization connects her earlier timing problem with a broader understanding of acting.
plans.method: Connect the difficulty at the first rehearsal to the change Aya makes by the ending.
plans.trap: A main idea should explain the change, rather than repeat one isolated detail.

plans.prompt: What can the reader infer from Aya’s decision to mark a pause in her script?
choices: She wants to remember a useful timing choice instead of focusing only on her spoken words.
She has forgotten all the words she previously memorized.
She wants Luis to stop asking his character’s question.
She plans to keep the cast from watching her scene.
reasons: The cafeteria practice teaches her the effect of waiting, and the margin mark preserves that choice.
She still knows her words; her new concern is their timing.
She has learned to let Luis finish, rather than prevent his question.
The cast watches at the director’s invitation, with no effort by Aya to stop it.
plans.evidence: At the next rehearsal, Aya marked a small pause in the margin of her page.
plans.why: The mark is direct evidence of her action; its purpose is inferred from the successful pause during the preceding practice.
plans.method: Connect the new action to the result of the practice that immediately precedes it.
plans.trap: An inference should connect stated events without inventing a new motive.

plans.prompt: Where do Aya and Luis practice during the break?
choices: In the empty cafeteria.
Beside Aya’s kitchen table.
In the crowded school hallway.
In the director’s office.
reasons: The passage directly names the empty cafeteria as their practice location.
Aya practices alone beside the kitchen table before the first rehearsal.
No hallway practice is described in the passage.
No director’s office is mentioned as a practice location.
plans.evidence: They took their scripts to the empty cafeteria during the break.
plans.why: This sentence explicitly answers the location question; the kitchen belongs to an earlier event.
plans.method: Locate the event and time named in the question before selecting its setting.
plans.trap: The passage may name several places; match the place to the correct event.

plans.prompt: As used in the final paragraph, what does “margin” mean?
choices: The blank area beside the written lines on a page.
The time remaining before a rehearsal ends.
A stage curtain separating the cast from the audience.
A different part of the play assigned to another actor.
reasons: Aya writes a mark beside the text of her script, so the page-border meaning fits.
The word names a place on the page, rather than an amount of time.
No curtain is used for the written reminder.
Aya keeps her existing part and marks its page.
plans.evidence: Aya marked a small pause in the margin of her page.
plans.why: The words “marked” and “page” identify a writable blank border as the context-specific meaning.
plans.method: Use the action and the object in the sentence to choose the relevant meaning of the word.
plans.trap: A word’s meaning must fit the sentence in which it appears.

passages.title: Tickets and Time
passages.content:
The following is an original fictional news feature.

The spring concert had more interested families than the auditorium had seats. In previous years, the school had distributed its free tickets from the office at seven in the morning. The line was easy to count, and the rule was easy to explain: the first people to arrive received the first tickets. To some members of the concert committee, that simplicity was the strongest reason to keep the system.

Violinist Mara Ortiz agreed that the rule was simple. She disagreed that simplicity settled the question of access. Her father began work before the office opened, and her grandmother could not stand in a line for an hour. “They wanted to be there,” she said. “They just couldn’t be here at seven.” She was not asking the school to count her family’s interest more highly than another family’s. She wanted interest to be distinguishable from the ability to wait at a particular time.

The committee considered an online drawing in which each family could request up to two seats during a week-long application period. A random drawing would determine which requests were filled if demand exceeded supply. Several members welcomed the change. Others pointed out that moving a line from the hallway to a website could introduce a different barrier: not every family had reliable internet access, and a form could be confusing even to someone who could reach it.

The revised proposal retained the drawing but added paper applications and help from office staff during several time periods. No family would gain an extra entry by using both methods. The committee also proposed a separate recording of the concert for those who did not receive seats. The recording would not replace the experience of attending, but it would let more families hear the performance.

When the committee approved the proposal for one concert, it did not announce that a fair system had been perfected. It promised to ask whether families could complete applications, whether the entry limit was enforced consistently, and which difficulties remained. Every method still allocated a limited number of seats. The change was in what a family had to do to be considered for one.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central point of this feature?
choices: Changing a ticket process can reduce one access barrier while requiring attention to others.
An equal drawing is sufficient by itself to make a ticket process accessible.
Recorded performances should replace in-person concerts to broaden participation.
A family’s ability to arrive early is the best measure of its interest in the concert.
reasons: The proposal addresses early waiting, internet access, and consistent entry limits while acknowledging limited seats.
The online drawing still raises internet-access and form-completion barriers, prompting paper routes and assistance.
The recording is an additional option; the author explicitly distinguishes it from attending.
Mara’s family example challenges equating interest with the ability to wait at seven in the morning.
plans.evidence: The change was in what a family had to do to be considered for one.
plans.why: The ending distinguishes changes in access to consideration from an impossible guarantee that everyone receives a seat.
plans.method: Trace the original barrier, the new barrier raised in response, and the final qualified proposal.
plans.trap: Do not confuse a fairer application process with a guarantee of the desired outcome.

plans.prompt: What can reasonably be inferred about why the revised proposal forbids extra entries through both application methods?
choices: It aims to provide different routes to the same opportunity rather than an advantage for using both routes.
The paper form is intended to give a second chance after an unsuccessful online entry.
The committee mainly wants to make online applications faster to process.
The proposal gives paper applicants priority to compensate for the difficulty of waiting in line.
reasons: Multiple access routes are retained, but equal entry limits prevent a double application from creating an extra chance.
The entry restriction prevents two applications from producing two chances; paper is an alternative route, not an extra chance.
The surrounding discussion concerns access and consistent limits, not processing speed.
Paper applicants enter the same drawing; no priority for that route is described.
plans.evidence: No family would gain an extra entry by using both methods.
plans.why: The stated limit, read with the purpose of providing alternative access, supports equal treatment across the two routes.
plans.method: Connect the operational rule to the access problem the proposal is trying to address.
plans.trap: Infer a rule’s purpose from its role in the proposal; do not invent universal misconduct.

plans.prompt: Why does the author include the objections to an online drawing?
choices: To show that replacing the old system could create an access problem that the committee still needed to address.
To explain why the committee should return to the early-morning line unchanged.
To argue that the auditorium’s limited capacity prevents any improvement to the application process.
To show that free tickets make families less interested in attending the concert.
reasons: The objections explain the paper option and staff assistance in the revised proposal.
The revised proposal retains the drawing and addresses the objections; it does not restore the old line.
The number of seats stays limited, but the proposal still changes access to consideration for a seat.
The concern is reliable internet and usable forms, not whether free admission reduces interest.
plans.evidence: moving a line from the hallway to a website could introduce a different barrier
plans.why: The objection advances the explanation by identifying a problem that leads to a concrete change in the proposal.
plans.method: Ask how the included objection changes the development of the policy discussion.
plans.trap: An objection may improve a proposal rather than cancel it.

plans.prompt: In the last paragraph, what does “allocated” mean?
choices: Distributed according to a process.
Reserved specifically for performers’ relatives.
Counted to estimate how much demand exists.
Kept unavailable until a later concert.
reasons: Each ticket method assigns the existing limited seats to some requests.
Allocated names the distribution process; no exclusive family reservation appears in the paragraph.
Counting demand helps plan a distribution, but allocating the seats means assigning them rather than merely counting requests.
The seats are assigned for the current concert; the word does not mean postponing their use.
plans.evidence: Every method still allocated a limited number of seats.
plans.why: The context concerns how existing places are assigned, not how more places are created.
plans.method: Use the object of the verb and the contrast with the changed application process.
plans.trap: Choose the meaning that fits what is being acted on.

plans.prompt: Which reason most directly supports offering both paper and online applications?
choices: Some families could face an internet-access or form-completion barrier even if a drawing eliminates early waiting.
Office staff could easily count the people in the old early-morning line.
A separate recording allows families without seats to hear the performance.
The auditorium has fewer seats than the number of interested families.
reasons: Alternative routes and assistance address the specific access concerns raised about moving the process online.
This explains an advantage of the old line but not why the revised system needs alternative application routes.
The recording addresses participation after seat distribution, not barriers to submitting a request.
Scarcity explains the need for an allocation method, but not the separate internet-access issue that paper forms address.
plans.evidence: not every family had reliable internet access, and a form could be confusing even to someone who could reach it.
plans.why: This concern explains why another route and help completing applications are relevant to the proposal.
plans.method: Match the proposed feature to the specific problem it is designed to address.
plans.trap: A reason for widening access is different from a promise to satisfy every request.

passages.title: A Fold in the Curtain
passages.content:
For twenty-eight years, Mr. Vale had opened the small theater by lifting its curtain cord three inches and listening. The first pull was not meant to raise the curtain; it told him whether the cord had settled into the groove or caught against the wooden guide. He could have explained the sound, but the explanation would have taken longer than the movement. On his final afternoon as stage manager, he made the familiar pull and waited for a familiar question that did not arrive.

The new stage manager, Tessa, stood beside the control board with a notebook closed under her arm. Mr. Vale had prepared three pages of instructions and, beneath them, a few sentences he thought he might say if someone asked what the theater had meant to him. Nobody had asked. The actors were changing costumes, the director was discussing a light cue, and a delivery driver wanted to know which door opened onto the street. It seemed, for a moment, an extraordinarily ordinary day on which to stop doing something he had done for most of his adult life.

Tessa crossed the stage and studied the curtain cord. “That little catch,” she said. “Is it the guide?” Mr. Vale nodded. She eased the cord sideways before pulling, then watched the heavy fabric rise without a scrape. He began to explain why the wood could not simply be sanded farther back, but she pointed toward the painted scene behind it. “Because the frame would show from the front row?” He looked toward the empty seats. He had once learned that by sitting in each of them.

At rehearsal, a young actor missed an entrance. Mr. Vale turned toward the passage behind the stage, already reaching for the flashlight that usually hung from his belt. Tessa was there before him, lighting the narrow step without speaking into the scene. The actor entered only a moment late. From the seats, the mistake would scarcely have been visible. Mr. Vale let his hand fall.

Afterward, Tessa asked him to sit in the front row while she checked the curtain. She did not ask for a final lecture or offer to frame his instructions. She asked whether the corner of the painted scene still showed when the fabric was lifted. He moved one seat to the left, then another, and raised a finger when he saw it. She adjusted the cord. On the second check, he shook his head.

His pages remained in his bag. Before leaving, he wrote one additional line at the bottom: “Check it from the seats.” It was less complete than the explanation he had planned, and more useful to the next afternoon. Tessa was still working when he reached the door. She called after him, not to bring him back but to ask whether he could attend opening night. He said he would like a seat near the front.

plans.prompt: Which statement best expresses the passage’s central idea?
choices: Mr. Vale comes to recognize that the theater can carry his practical knowledge forward without making his departure a grand ceremony.
Mr. Vale becomes disappointed because Tessa ignores the technical knowledge he offers to share.
An experienced worker gains lasting recognition mainly by leaving exhaustive written instructions.
A personal departure matters only when coworkers formally acknowledge it with a ceremony.
reasons: His disappointment at the ordinary day gives way to collaboration, a practical note, and an invitation to return as an audience member.
Tessa notices the cord’s catch, understands the visible frame, and asks Mr. Vale to help check the view.
The ending values one practical addition over the complete explanation he had prepared.
Mr. Vale comes to value useful continuity and accepts an invitation without receiving the expected ceremony.
plans.evidence: It was less complete than the explanation he had planned, and more useful to the next afternoon.
plans.why: The practical addition replaces the anticipated ceremonial explanation and points toward the next person’s continuing work.
plans.method: Connect the opening expectation of acknowledgment to the ending’s emphasis on useful continuity.
plans.trap: A central idea should account for the change in the character’s understanding, not invent others’ motives.

plans.prompt: What does Mr. Vale’s decision to let his hand fall during the missed entrance most strongly suggest?
choices: He recognizes that Tessa has already handled a task he habitually took responsibility for.
He is embarrassed because the rehearsal reveals that he has forgotten the entrance routine.
He decides to leave the actor unaided so that the actor will learn through a mistake.
He concludes that assisting entrances had never been part of his responsibility.
reasons: His reaching motion begins an old routine, but Tessa is already lighting the step, so he stops.
He instinctively reaches toward his usual flashlight, showing that the routine is familiar; no embarrassment about forgetting is stated.
The actor is already being assisted by Tessa; the stopped movement follows her intervention.
His habitual response shows that this was a task he used to perform, not an unfamiliar duty.
plans.evidence: Tessa was there before him, lighting the narrow step without speaking into the scene.
plans.why: The stated action directly establishes that the task is being performed; his recognition of this is the supported inference behind the stopped movement.
plans.method: Read the physical action with the event immediately preceding it, distinguishing a habitual response from an unsupported emotional motive.
plans.trap: Infer only what the visible action and its immediate context support.

plans.prompt: How does Mr. Vale’s attitude change over the course of the passage?
choices: He shifts from waiting for a special acknowledgment to accepting a practical role in the theater’s continuing work.
He becomes dependent on Tessa because he no longer understands how the theater works.
He grows more insistent on receiving a formal tribute after Tessa helps the actor.
He resolves his disappointment by refusing to return to the theater after retirement.
reasons: He begins with prepared remarks and an expected question, then helps check the sightline and leaves a useful instruction.
His seat-by-seat check remains useful and reflects detailed understanding of the theater’s sightlines.
He leaves a short practical note instead of insisting on his prepared remarks or a ceremony.
He agrees to attend opening night and asks for a seat near the front.
plans.evidence: Before leaving, he wrote one additional line at the bottom: “Check it from the seats.”
plans.why: The new brief instruction shows a turn from explaining his own importance toward helping the next person perform the work.
plans.method: Compare what the character expects at the beginning with what he chooses to contribute at the end.
plans.trap: A quiet change in action may reveal development more reliably than an explicit declaration.

plans.prompt: What does the curtain cord most strongly represent within the passage?
choices: Practical knowledge that becomes useful through attentive action and can be passed to another person.
A ceremonial link requiring the next manager to keep every older method unchanged.
Mr. Vale’s desire to control performances after leaving the theater.
An obstacle that only Mr. Vale understands and must remove before he can leave.
reasons: Both stage managers use the cord attentively, and its effect must be checked from the seats.
Tessa adjusts the cord, showing responsive craft rather than a rigid requirement to preserve every method.
Mr. Vale lets Tessa act and contributes an inspection principle, rather than asserting continuing control.
Tessa recognizes the guide’s catch and understands its visual consequence, so the knowledge is not exclusive to him.
plans.evidence: She eased the cord sideways before pulling, then watched the heavy fabric rise without a scrape.
plans.why: Tessa’s use of the familiar tool shows that the craft depends on observation and adjustment, rather than possession by one person.
plans.method: Trace how both characters use the object and what its repeated role reveals about their relationship.
plans.trap: A symbol’s meaning must come from its actions and context, not an arbitrary association.

plans.prompt: Which description best captures the narration’s tone toward Mr. Vale’s departure?
choices: Restrained and sympathetic, with attention to small actions that carry emotional significance.
Nostalgic and indignant about Tessa replacing traditions without respect.
Detached and technical, concerned only with correct operating procedures.
Dramatic and accusatory toward the workers who do not arrange a ceremony.
reasons: The narration notices his prepared remarks, habitual reaching motion, and revised note without forcing a dramatic speech.
The narrative is sensitive to the departure, but Tessa respects and continues practical knowledge rather than rejecting it.
Technical actions carry emotional meaning through Mr. Vale’s expectations and changing response.
The narration gives ordinary details and quiet shifts without accusing the workers or staging a dramatic confrontation.
plans.evidence: It seemed, for a moment, an extraordinarily ordinary day on which to stop doing something he had done for most of his adult life.
plans.why: The contrast conveys the emotional scale of the departure gently, without ridicule or melodramatic alarm.
plans.method: Connect the narrator’s access to the character’s expectations with the restrained way the details are presented.
plans.trap: Tone emerges from how details are framed, not only from whether the subject is sad or happy.
